Any discussion of atomism in Arab-Islamic thought would remain incomplete without considering the position of Ibrāhīm ibn Sayyār al-Naẓẓām. This major Muʿtazilite thinker, together with the intellectual current that influenced him, represents an important stage in the development of philosophical thought before Arab-Islamic philosophy emerged in a form independent of the school of kalām.

Al-Naẓẓām lived during the most flourishing period of Muʿtazilite thought and took an active part in its intellectual and theoretical work. He also helped organize the questions studied by kalām in a way that developed both their intellectual content and the methods used to investigate them. Over time, these inquiries acquired a coherent set of principles and rules, allowing kalām to take shape as a distinct field of knowledge with principles of its own.

One reason al-Naẓẓām was able to occupy such an important position in the intellectual life of his age seems to have been his close engagement with earlier cultures, both Eastern and Greek. He was widely acquainted with the Greek philosophy that had reached Arab-Islamic thought during the eighth and ninth centuries.

The early historians of Islamic sects give us plenty of evidence for the depth of this connection, especially his connection with Greek philosophy. Even the titles of the books they attribute to him make this clear.

Al-Ashʿarī, for example, mentions two of his books. One is The Book of the Particle, which, as we understand al-Ashʿarī, presented the views of Muslim thinkers on the question of the “indivisible particle.” The other is Motion, or The Motion of Bodies.
Al-Ashʿarī quotes al-Naẓẓām as saying in this work:

All bodies are in motion. Motion is of two kinds: motion of impulse and motion from one place to another. All bodies are therefore truly in motion, even though ordinary language may describe them as being at rest. Motions are nothing other than being itself.

Al-Baghdādī also attributes to him a Book of Generation (al-Farq bayna al-Firaq, p. 117). Al-Khayyāṭ mentions a book by him on divine unity (al-Intiṣār, p. 172). Ibn al-Murtaḍā, in al-Munya wa-l-Amal, mentions a work entitled Refutation of Aristotle. And there were others.
As for al-Naẓẓām’s theory of atoms, the historians of the Islamic sects agree that his position set him apart from the other Muʿtazilites. He rejected the idea of an “indivisible particle.”

Al-Shahrastānī says that this position brought al-Naẓẓām closer to the philosophers. Al-Ashʿarī reports him as saying that every part has another part, every portion has another portion, and every half has another half. A part can therefore always be divided again, with no final end to the process of division.

Al-Khayyāṭ, however, interprets al-Naẓẓām’s infinite division as something that happens only in the mind, rather than as an actual physical division. He bases this interpretation on al-Naẓẓām himself:
What Ibrāhīm denied was that bodies are made up of parts that cannot themselves be divided. He held that there is no body that the mind cannot imagine dividing into two halves.

But the objection raised against al-Naẓẓām by his contemporaries suggests that they understood him differently. They seem to have taken his theory of infinite division to mean actual division, not merely division in the imagination.
Al-Naẓẓām’s own reply to their objection supports this reading, as we will now see.
Al-Naẓẓām’s theory of infinite division immediately raised a problem.
If the parts of a body can be divided without end, what happens when an ant walks across a rock from one side to the other?

The ant is finite. But according to al-Naẓẓām’s theory, the parts of the rock are infinitely divisible. That would seem to mean that something finite—the ant—has crossed something infinite. And that appears impossible.
Al-Naẓẓām answered this objection by introducing another idea that completed, or at least explained, his theory of infinite division. This became known as the theory of the leap.
The ant crosses some of the rock’s parts by walking and crosses others by leaping over them.

Al-Naẓẓām compared this to a rope stretched over a horizontal beam in the middle of a well. The rope is fifty cubits long and carries a bucket. Another rope, also fifty cubits long, has a hook attached to it and is used to pull the first rope. In this way, the bucket reaches the top of the well after covering a distance of one hundred cubits, even though the rope itself is only fifty cubits long and the movement takes place in the same period of time.
Al-Naẓẓām’s explanation was that part of the distance had been covered by a leap.

Al-Naẓẓām failed to realize that a leap also crosses a distance corresponding to another distance. The difficulty therefore remains. The only difference between walking and leaping lies in how quickly or slowly the movement takes place.
Al-Ashʿarī gives a somewhat different account of al-Naẓẓām’s theory:

Al-Naẓẓām claimed that a body may be in one place and then move to a third place without passing through the second. This happens by way of a leap. He used several examples to support the idea, including a spinning top. Its upper part moves more than its lower part and covers more distance. Al-Naẓẓām said that this happens because its upper part moves alongside things that the part below it had not previously faced.

By the last sentence, al-Naẓẓām seems to mean that the upper part of the spinning top moves more freely than the lower part and meets less resistance. The upper part reaches things first, before pressure and obstruction have accumulated enough to slow its movement.
Al-Ashʿarī himself simply reports the theory in this form. He does not state his own view of it. Instead, he records the replies made by other theologians.
Among them were Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf and others, who argued that:

It is impossible for a body to arrive at a place without passing through what comes before it. This cannot happen. A body may, however, have one part at rest while most of it is moving. A horse, even while walking or running hard, has tiny moments of rest as it places and lifts its feet. This is why one horse may be slower than another. A stone rolling downward likewise has tiny moments of rest, and this is why it may move more slowly than another, heavier stone released beside it.

Al-Ashʿarī also reports that many speculative thinkers believed that, if two stones are released together, the heavier one will move faster. Their explanation was that the lighter stone meets more obstacles. It is pushed to the right and left, forward and backward, while the heavier stone continues downward during the moments when the lighter one is being deflected. The heavier stone therefore reaches the bottom sooner.
Al-Baghdādī and Ibn al-Murtaḍā describe al-Naẓẓām’s theory of the leap in much the same way as al-Shahrastānī.

Taken together, these different accounts of the theory, and the objections made against it, suggest that al-Naẓẓām believed in an actual infinite division of matter, not merely a possible or imaginary division in the mind.

Consider the form of the original objection. The ant crosses the parts of the rock from one side to the other. If those parts can be divided without end, then something finite—the ant—has crossed something infinite.
Then consider al-Naẓẓām’s reply: his example of a fifty-cubit rope somehow covering one hundred cubits, followed by his further example of the spinning top.

All of this shows that the debate between al-Naẓẓām and his opponents was based on the idea of an actual, physical, infinite division. It was not about an infinite division that existed only in thought.

If al-Naẓẓām had meant only an imaginary division—one existing in the mind rather than in reality, or existing only as a possibility rather than in actuality—there would have been no need for these concrete physical examples.
Indeed, if imaginary division had been all he meant, he would have had no need for the theory of the leap at all.
The whole idea of the leap rests on a theory of motion understood as something real and actual, not imaginary.
So what was al-Naẓẓām’s theory of motion?
Al-Shahrastānī and al-Ashʿarī give us our two best sources for this theory.
Among the views that al-Shahrastānī says distinguished al-Naẓẓām from the other Muʿtazilites was this:

All human actions are nothing but motions. Rest is a motion of impulse. Acts of knowledge and acts of will are motions of the soul. By “motion” he did not mean only motion from one place to another. He understood motion as the beginning of some kind of change, as the philosophers did when they spoke of motion in quality, quantity, position, place, time, and the other categories.
This passage makes it clear that al-Naẓẓām regarded motion as the form taken by every human action, including acts of consciousness such as knowing and willing, which he called “motions of the soul.”

He also seems to have treated rest as a form of motion. He called it a “motion of impulse,” apparently meaning a hidden internal motion within the act itself. He may have had in mind a kind of inner self-propelling force that also resists whatever obstructs outward movement.
Al-Shahrastānī says that al-Naẓẓām “did not mean motion from one place to another” and that, for him, “motion is the beginning of some kind of change.”

This seems to suggest that, when al-Naẓẓām speaks of the motion involved in human actions, he is referring specifically to what Aristotle placed under the category of quality. Movement from one place to another, by contrast, belongs to the category of place.
Al-Shahrastānī’s text appears to rule out this second meaning from what al-Naẓẓām intended.

This may agree in some respects with Aristotle. Aristotle often uses the word “change” specifically for qualitative change, even though his wider concept of motion includes the different forms of becoming covered by all ten Aristotelian categories. In its broad sense, change itself includes all these different kinds of motion, which in Aristotle are really general forms of being.
If this reading of al-Shahrastānī is correct, and if al-Naẓẓām really did restrict human action to qualitative motion, then al-Shahrastānī has contradicted himself.

On the one hand, he tells us that al-Naẓẓām did not mean movement from one place to another, which belongs to the category of place. But on the other hand, he also says that al-Naẓẓām followed the philosophers in recognizing motion in “quality, quantity, position, place, time, and so on.”

In any case, al-Shahrastānī’s passage alone does not give us al-Naẓẓām’s complete theory of motion. It deals only with human actions. We still need to know what al-Naẓẓām thought about motion in bodies and in the other material forms found in the world.
Al-Ashʿarī fills this gap in several passages of his Maqālāt al-Islāmiyyīn.
He first reports al-Naẓẓām as saying:

All bodies are in motion. Motion is of two kinds: motion of impulse and motion from one place to another. All bodies are therefore truly moving, though in ordinary language they may be called still. Motions are nothing other than being.

I also read in a book attributed to al-Naẓẓām that he said: “I do not know what rest is, unless it means that a thing remained in the same place for two moments—in other words, that it moved there for two moments.”
He also held that when God creates bodies, they are already moving with a motion of impulse.
This passage gives us several important parts of al-Naẓẓām’s theory.
First, it shows how broad and unified the theory was. Motion appears here as something absolute, while rest appears as something relative.
In his treatment of motion and rest, al-Naẓẓām therefore begins from a position that contains a materialist and dialectical tendency, even though it remains inside a metaphysical framework.
In fact, the philosophical importance of his view becomes especially clear within that very framework.

To say that bodies are already moving with an internal motion when God creates them means that al-Naẓẓām has managed to push through the metaphysical barrier at precisely the point where it is strongest: the idea of divine creation itself.
Even while retaining that idea, he is moving toward the recognition of an objective motion within matter itself.
In other words, al-Naẓẓām comes close here to treating matter as a philosophical category in its own right.

Now add this view—that matter has an objective motion even at the moment when it is created from outside—to the position we discussed earlier: that bodies are made up of atoms, substances, or particles that can be divided endlessly in reality, not merely in the imagination, as al-Khayyāṭ claimed in al-Intiṣār.

Taken together, these ideas allow us to see an early form of philosophical thinking about matter and its objective motion. Within a wider framework that remains idealist and metaphysical, a materialist and dialectical position begins to shine through.

We should now return to al-Shahrastānī’s earlier statement and look more closely at his report that, for al-Naẓẓām, all human actions are motions; that acts of knowledge and will are also motions, even if he calls them “motions of the soul”; and that motion is the beginning of change.
If we combine these statements with al-Ashʿarī’s account—that all bodies are moving and that motions are nothing other than being—we can draw out a remarkably unified view, especially for its time.

Al-Naẓẓām seems to be trying to discover that motion is the form in which matter exists and continues to exist, and that motion is therefore a property inseparable from matter. Matter does not exist without motion.
He also seems to be moving toward an understanding of the relationship between thought and matter, since he treats acts of knowledge and will themselves as motions.

The fact that this attempt appeared within a religious form of thought does not reduce its importance. On the contrary, that historical setting is part of what gives the attempt both its intellectual and historical value.

We can see the point more clearly if we remember that al-Naẓẓām’s theory included every kind of continual change in the things and phenomena of the universe, from the simplest forms of change to the most complex of all: thought itself.
We should also remember that modern experimental science, through its great achievements, has confirmed the objective reality of this truth.
Al-Naẓẓām also moved far away from the metaphysical understanding of rest when he rejected the idea that rest means the absence of motion.
As we saw, al-Ashʿarī reports him as saying:
I do not know what rest is, unless it means that a thing remained in the same place for two moments—in other words, that it moved there for two moments.
Al-Naẓẓām is therefore insisting that matter can never be separated from motion. Rest exists only in an apparent and conventional sense.

In this way, he comes close to the scientific dialectical view, which does not accept the complete absence of motion and recognizes rest only as something relative. A body may be described as being at rest in relation to another body at a particular moment, while in reality it is still moving.
This also sets al-Naẓẓām apart in an important way from his fellow major Muʿtazilite thinker Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf.
Their disagreement was not limited to the question of the indivisible particle. It also concerned motion and rest.

Abū al-Hudhayl held that bodies can truly move and truly be at rest, and that motion and rest are different from being itself. At the moment when God creates a body, he said, it is neither at rest nor in motion.
Scientific method requires us not to look at al-Naẓẓām’s views on motion and the infinite division of matter in isolation from his views on other questions.
If we did that, we would make a serious mistake both in our method and in the conclusions we draw.
We therefore need to follow the strong materialist tendency we have seen in al-Naẓẓām across his other ideas as well. We need to ask how far the same logic runs through his thought as a whole.
Did this distinctive thinker really have a coherent and connected intellectual system?
Or was the materialist tendency we have seen so far no more than a passing idea, unrelated to other scattered philosophical thoughts that were themselves equally temporary and disconnected?
To answer this, we need to examine several of al-Naẓẓām’s positions on questions that were widely discussed and disputed among the theologians of his time.
A — Al-Naẓẓām held that it is impossible for something in motion to move “in nothing” or “toward nothing.”
